newsitem.title: HONG KONG: American business group optimistic about Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: American business group optimistic about Hong Kong.

text.p: More American business people in Hong Kong are optimistic about their future in the territory than two years ago despite the imminent unification with China, the American Chamber of Commerce said on Tuesday.

A survey of members showed that 95 percent of respondents thought the business climate in Hong Kong would remain favourable or very favourable over the next five years following Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on July 1.
A similar survey conducted in 1995 showed a 91-percent favourable response to the same question.
More than half of the American chamber's 2,800 members responded to the survey this year.

American chamber president Douglas Henck said the optimism was based on a number of factors, including Hong Kong's long integration with southern China and a commitment to keeping Hong Kong's civil service, taxes and trade regime intact.

"In my view, the negative perspective of Hong Kong in the Western media comes not from an intention to be negative but rather from the fact that these things which stay the same are not news," Henck said.
But he conceded that, despite their overall optimism, American business people were concerned about the rule of law, free flow of information and the cost of doing business.

The survey apparently touched on a possible rise in corruption, cited by a British chamber of commerce survey as a leading concern among its members and mentioned in other surveys as a major issue for local people.
Henck said the American business community's overall optimism about the future in Hong Kong was rooted in a solid understanding of Hong Kong history.
"If you study Hong Kong's history you will see how Hong Kong and its people have come shining through every crisis. You will see why there should be optimism," Henck said.

Francis Ho, Hong Kong's director general of industry, said the government would continue its present policy of minimum intervention towards the development of its manufacturing and service industries.
"We subscribe totally to the market-driven approach and are determined that business decisions should be left to the businessmen," Ho said.
"Hong Kong prides itself on the fact that it has one of the world's most liberalised investment regimes."
Government intervention to support Hong Kong's regional competitiveness has become a hot topic in the territory as it speeds towards unification with China on July 1.
